Unit 1. What a prompt is and how Claude reads it

On the board: before you can engineer a prompt, you need three facts. What a prompt is made of. How the model reads it. What it costs to send it.

You will leave this unit able to define a token, a prompt, and a language model in one sentence each. You will also describe what happens between your API call and the answer.

What a prompt is

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. A prompt is everything you send to the model in one request: the system instructions, the conversation messages, the tool definitions, and any retrieved documents. It is not just the user's question. It is the model's entire world for that request.

A large language model (LLM) is a system trained to do one thing: predict the next token, over and over, until the answer is complete. A token is a chunk of text the model reads and writes, roughly three to four characters of English. The word "unbelievable" is three tokens: un, believ, able.

How to read this diagram
  1. The three boxes are the tokens of one word: "un", "believ", "able". The model never sees the word as a unit. It sees the sequence of chunks.
  2. About four characters per token is the rule of thumb for English. Code and other languages split differently, but the counting unit is always the token.
  3. Why it matters: prices are per million tokens, windows use tokens as the unit, and output costs five times input (Unit 2). Token thinking starts here.

How Claude reads it

Rung 2: one level deeper. Your request has two parts. The system field carries standing instructions (Unit 4 covers what goes in it). The messages list carries the conversation: user turns, assistant turns, and tool results. Claude joins all of it into one long token sequence, reads it start to finish, then writes the answer one token at a time.

Three facts about this reading that shape everything else in this domain:

  1. The model is stateless. Each request stands alone. Claude does not remember your last request unless you send the history again. That is why turn 20 of a chat re-sends turns 1 through 19, and why long conversations get expensive (Unit 5 works out the math).
  2. Input and output have separate prices. Input tokens cost the list price. Output tokens cost five times more on every tier (Unit 2). Anything that makes the model write more, including step-by-step reasoning, pays the 5x rate.
  3. What you send is what it knows. If a fact is not in the prompt, Claude cannot use it. Retrieval, tools, and examples are not extras. They are how knowledge gets into the only input channel the model has.
How to read this diagram
  1. Left boxes: the three ingredients of every request: system (standing rules), messages (the conversation so far), tools and retrieved documents.
  2. Center (one token sequence): Claude merges all three into a single stream of tokens. Order matters here, which is why Unit 6 cares where you put things.
  3. Right (answer): the model predicts one token, appends it, predicts the next. Reasoning and final text are both output tokens, both billed at the 5x rate.
  4. The stateless note: nothing persists between requests on the model's side. The "conversation" is your code re-sending the history each turn.
How they will ask this

Scenario shape: a question about why a follow-up message "forgot" earlier context, or what counts toward the token bill.

The trap: answers that assume the model remembers between requests, or that you pay only for the latest user message. The credited answer names the stateless request: you re-send history, you pay for the whole prompt, and nothing outside the prompt exists for the model.

Next: Unit 2, the Claude model family: who is who, and the price pattern to memorize.

Unit 2. The Claude model family: who is who

Why this unit comes next.

Unit 1 showed how Claude reads a prompt: instructions, examples, and context compete for attention inside one window. That leaves a practical question open: which model should read it? This unit introduces the four tiers, so every later choice carries a price tag.

On the board: a team asks which Claude model to standardize on. How do you compare the four tiers, and what does each one cost you?

You will leave this unit able to name the four current tiers. You will know their price and context numbers, and the one-line job each tier is built for.

What the family is

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. Claude is a family of large language models from Anthropic. Think of it like a car lineup: same brand and fueling system (one API), four engines tuned for different jobs. Every current model takes text and image input, produces text output, and supports tool use (calling functions you provide, such as a search API), vision, and multilingual work.

The differences are intelligence, speed, context window size, and price. A context window is the total number of tokens the model can consider in one request. Unit 5 teaches you to budget it.

As of the docs snapshot, the lineup is:
Model Built for Input / MTok Output / MTok Context window Max output Speed
Claude Fable 5.1 Demanding reasoning, long-horizon agentic work $10 $50 1M tokens 128K Slowest
Claude Opus 5.5 Long-running agentic coding and knowledge work $4 $20 1M tokens 128K Moderate
Claude Sonnet 5 Best speed and intelligence balance $2 $10 1M tokens 128K Fast
Claude Haiku 4.5 Fastest, near-frontier intelligence $1 $5 200K tokens 64K Fastest

MTok = per million tokens. Prices from docs.anthropic.com, verified 2026-09-28. Docs advise: start with Opus 5.5 for most workloads. Reach for Fable 5.1 only when evals on Opus at higher effort still fall short.

Why four tiers exist

Intelligence costs compute. A harder reasoning problem needs a bigger model, more thinking time, or both, and the provider passes that cost to you. If every task ran on the smartest model, simple work (classify this ticket, extract these fields) would burn ten times the money it needs. The tiers let you match the engine to the load.

Haiku fits high-volume simple work. Sonnet is the everyday default. Opus fits sustained agentic coding. Fable fits the hardest reasoning.

One warning for the exam: "bigger model means better answers for everything" is the favorite D2 trap. On simple, well-specified tasks (classification, extraction, formatting), a smaller model with good prompting often matches the big one. The big model's edge shows up on multi-step reasoning and novel problems. Paying for intelligence you do not use is the most common waste in production LLM budgets.

How to read this diagram
  1. Each card is one tier with its price and the job it fits. Haiku: high-volume simple work. Sonnet: the everyday default. Opus: sustained agentic coding. Fable: the hardest reasoning.
  2. Intelligence costs compute. Running simple work on the smartest model burns money for judgment you do not use.
  3. Takeaway: the red banner names the favorite D2 trap. On simple, well-specified tasks, a smaller model with good prompting often matches the big one.

The price pattern to memorize

Rung 2: one level deeper. Output tokens cost exactly five times input tokens on every current model ($10 vs $2, $5 vs $1, and so on). This ratio never moves. It matters because anything that makes the model write more (long answers, chain-of-thought reasoning, verbose thinking) pays the 5x rate. Keep this in your head for Units 3 and 6.

Haiku   $1 in  /  $5 out     \
Sonnet  $2 in  / $10 out      }  output = 5x input, on EVERY tier
Opus    $4 in  / $20 out      }  more writing = taxed at the 5x rate
Fable  $10 in  / $50 out     /

How to read this diagram
  1. Read left to right as a ladder: Haiku (cheapest, fastest) up to Fable (smartest, slowest, priciest).
  2. The rising bars above the row show intelligence: Fable tallest, Haiku shortest but still tall (docs call it near-frontier).
  3. The shrinking arrows below show speed: Haiku fastest, Fable slowest.
  4. The coin icons show relative price: each step roughly doubles to quintuples cost per token.
  5. Teaching point: the ladder is a menu, not a ranking. The architect's job is to pick the lowest rung that clears the quality bar (Unit 8).
How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "A support triage bot classifies 2M tickets a month. Current prototype on Opus 5.5 hits 94% accuracy. The requirement is 90%. Latency budget 800 ms." Trap: options include staying on Opus ("it already works") or jumping to Fable ("highest accuracy"). The credited move is to test Haiku/Sonnet against the 90% bar, because the requirement is already met and the current choice burns money.

Read as constraint-first: the credited answer is almost never "use the biggest model". It is the tier whose measured quality clears the bar at the lowest cost and latency. One distractor to memorize: Haiku's 200K window (vs 1M elsewhere) and its 64K max output. Scenarios that need more context quietly disqualify Haiku.

Next: Unit 3, zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought.

Unit 3. Zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought

Why this unit comes next.

Unit 2 gave you the lineup and its price pattern. But a model is only as good as the prompt it receives. This unit covers the three core techniques: zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought, plus when each one earns its tokens.

On the board: three ways to ask a model to do a task. When does each one help, and when is each one just burning tokens?

You will leave this unit able to choose the technique per task and price the cost of reasoning.

The three techniques

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. Three ways to ask, in order of cost. Zero-shot means asking directly with no examples. Example: "Classify this ticket as billing, technical, or account." Few-shot means showing a handful of input-output examples first, so the model copies the pattern.

Chain-of-thought (CoT) means asking the model to reason step by step before answering. Move right only when the task's difficulty demands it.

ZERO-SHOT:   prompt -------------------> answer            (cheapest, default)
FEW-SHOT:    prompt + 2-5 examples -----> answer            (fixes format/judgment)
CHAIN-OF-THOUGHT: prompt + reasoning --> answer            (multi-step reasoning only)

When each one helps

Rung 2: one level deeper. Match the technique to the task, not to habit:

  • Zero-shot: the task is clear and the model already knows the pattern. Classification with obvious categories, extraction of named fields, simple rewrites. Cheapest option. Always try this first.
  • Few-shot: the output format or judgment is non-obvious. A house style for summaries, edge-case labeling rules, mapping messy inputs to a strict schema. Two to five examples usually do it. More examples have diminishing returns and each one costs input tokens on every request (though examples cache well, since they are static).
  • Chain-of-thought: the task needs multi-step reasoning. Math word problems, planning, debugging, comparing options with trade-offs. This is where the big quality gains come from, and where Fable and high-effort Opus earn their price.
How to read this diagram
  1. Start at the top: ask what the task demands, then follow the line down. Each card's first line is the condition that selects it.
  2. Zero-shot is the default first try. Few-shot fixes non-obvious formats. Chain-of-thought is for multi-step reasoning, where the big quality gains and the big token bills live.
  3. Takeaway: more examples have diminishing returns, and each one costs input tokens on every request.
How to read this diagram
  1. The waste row: simple high-volume task plus CoT equals waste. Pick zero-shot or few-shot.
  2. The earn row: novel multi-step reasoning plus a quality bar. Use CoT or extended thinking with a stronger model.
  3. Token economics: few-shot costs input tokens, which are cheap and cacheable. CoT costs output tokens, at the 5x rate.
  4. The exam tests whether the technique earns its tokens against the constraint.

When chain-of-thought wastes tokens

The expensive habit. Chain-of-thought is the costliest of the three techniques, because reasoning tokens are output tokens. Knowing when not to use it saves more than knowing how.

Rung 3: the full picture: the cost math. CoT generates reasoning as output tokens, and output costs 5x input on every model. On tasks where zero-shot already works (classify, extract, format), CoT adds cost and latency for no quality gain. It can even hurt. Longer reasoning chains give the model more room to talk itself into a wrong answer. The exam loves this: a scenario where someone added "think step by step" to a classification prompt, and the credited action is to remove it.

Worked cost example. Sonnet 5, one million requests a day, each with 500 extra thinking tokens. The math: 500 × $10/M = $0.005 per request just for the thinking. That is $5,000 a day. If the task is simple extraction that zero-shot handles at the same accuracy, that $5,000 buys nothing.

Extended thinking (the built-in kind, controlled by an effort or budget setting) follows the same economics: thinking blocks consume context and budget. Unit 5 shows the mechanism: thinking is output, and output competes with your context window and your wallet at the same time.

How to read this diagram
  1. Left lane (zero-shot): prompt goes straight to answer. Fewest tokens, fastest. Default choice.
  2. Middle lane (few-shot): example chips sit between prompt and answer. The checkmark means format adherence improves. Costs input tokens, which are cheap and cacheable.
  3. Right lane (chain-of-thought): reasoning boxes stack up before the answer. The coin stack flags the cost: reasoning is output tokens at the 5x rate.
  4. Teaching point: move right only when the task's difficulty demands it, and measure that the quality gain is real.
How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "A form-field extraction pipeline uses chain-of-thought on every request. Accuracy is 99.1% with or without it. The bill tripled after the team added CoT." Trap: answers that keep CoT and switch models, or add caching to "fix" the cost. The credited move is to drop CoT (it adds no accuracy here) and verify with the eval, because the cost comes from output tokens that caching cannot discount.

Pair each technique with its constraint: simple, high-volume task plus CoT equals waste: pick zero-shot or few-shot. Novel multi-step reasoning plus a quality bar equals CoT or extended thinking, preferably on a stronger model. And remember the few-shot sweet spot: format problems are usually solved with examples, not with a bigger model.

Next: Unit 4, system prompts: the constitution of your application.

Unit 4. System prompts: the constitution of your application

Why this unit comes next.

Unit 3 taught techniques you apply per request. Do not retype instructions you repeat on every request. This unit answers where standing instructions live: the system prompt, the constitution of your application.

On the board: every request to your agent needs the same rules, role, and output format. Where do you put them so they apply every time, without retyping by hand?

You will leave this unit able to design a system prompt, templatize it, and explain where prompt guardrails stop being enough.

How to read this diagram
  1. The example is form-field extraction with chain-of-thought on every request. Accuracy is 99.1 percent with CoT and 99.1 percent without it.
  2. The bill: reasoning is output tokens at the 5x rate. The bill tripled for zero gain.
  3. Caching cannot discount output. Cache hits cut input cost only. Output always bills full.
  4. The credited move: drop CoT and verify with the eval. The exam rewards the cheaper sufficient technique.

What a system prompt is

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. A system prompt is a block of instructions sent with every API request, before the conversation. It is the model's standing orders: who it is, what job it does, what rules it follows, what its answers should look like. The user never sees it, but it shapes every response. One API detail worth knowing: the request has a dedicated system field, separate from the messages list, precisely so these standing orders stay stable across turns.

Why it exists

Without one, you would paste the same instructions into every user message: role, rules, format, tone. That is error-prone (someone forgets), wasteful (you pay for those tokens on every request), and uncacheable in a messy way. A system prompt centralizes the constants of your application in one versioned place.

How to read this diagram
  1. The blue panel is the dedicated system field: role, job, rules, and answer format. It stays stable across turns while the messages list changes.
  2. Without it, you would paste the same instructions into every user message: error-prone, wasteful, and messy to cache.
  3. Takeaway: the system prompt centralizes the constants of your application in one versioned place.
How to read this diagram
  1. The system card holds role, job, rules, and answer format. It stays stable across turns, and you version, review, and cache it. It is the constitution of your app.
  2. The user card holds the live input for this turn. It changes every request. Never put standing rules here.
  3. Without the system field you would paste the same instructions into every user message. That is error-prone, wasteful, and messy to cache.
  4. What breaks: standing rules in the user message. They drift, they cost, and caching cannot help.

Anatomy of a good system prompt

Rung 2: one level deeper. Build it in layers, most stable first:

As you learned in D1, the translation method turns a vague ask into a spec. The system prompt is where that spec lives.

  1. Identity. "You are a claims-review assistant for an insurance company." One or two sentences. Sets the role the model plays.
  2. Task scope. What it does and, just as important, what it does not do. "Review claim summaries for completeness. Do not approve or deny claims."
  3. Rules and constraints. The non-negotiables. "Cite the policy section for every finding. Never invent a policy number."
  4. Output format. The exact shape you want: JSON schema, headings, length limits. Models follow explicit format specs far better than hints.
  5. Guardrails. Refusal and escalation behavior. "If the input contains personal data beyond the claim ID, stop and ask for a redacted copy."
  6. Edge-case handling. What to do when inputs are ambiguous or contradictory. This is where most system prompts earn their keep.

Keep it tight. You pay for every token in the system prompt on every request, so bloat is a recurring tax. Put the highest-value instructions first and cut anything the model already does well by default. Longer is not safer: past a point, extra instructions dilute attention, and contradictory instructions ("be concise" plus "explain thoroughly") make behavior less predictable, not more. A short prompt whose rules do not fight each other beats a long one.

How to read this diagram
  1. Read top to bottom: identity, scope, rules, format, guardrails. Stability decreases downward, so put the most permanent content highest.
  2. The bracket on the left marks the cached static prefix: everything above the user message that never changes between requests is cacheable.
  3. The divider line is the architectural boundary: above it is your constitution (versioned, reviewed, cached). Below it is the live input (variable, uncached).
  4. Teaching point: guardrails sit in the prompt, but a prompt is not a security boundary (see the misunderstanding below).

Prompt templates

Rung 3: the full picture. A prompt template is a system prompt with slots: placeholders filled in per request or per deployment. Example slots: {{customer_tier}}, {{policy_version}}, {{output_language}}. Templates let one reviewed prompt serve many configurations without copy-paste drift. Treat templates like code: version them in source control, review changes, and test the rendered prompt, not just the template.

One caution for caching (Unit 6): a slot that changes per request (a timestamp, a user ID) changes the prompt prefix and can silently kill your cache hit rate. Put volatile slots at the end, after everything stable. (The cost reason arrives in Unit 6: a caching technique discounts only the stable prefix.)

How to read this diagram
  1. The gray box is a template: static text with slots like customer tier and policy version filled in per request or per deployment.
  2. Treat templates like code: version them, review changes, and test the rendered prompt, not just the template.
  3. Takeaway: a slot that changes per request, like a timestamp or user ID, silently kills the cache hit rate. Put volatile slots at the end.

Prompt guardrails, and their limit

The honest limit. A system prompt can steer behavior, but it is still just text the model reads. This section is clear about where guardrails stop working.

Guardrails here means behavioral rules written in the prompt: refuse disallowed requests, escalate ambiguous ones, validate output shape. They are cheap and effective for steering normal behavior.

Their limit: a prompt instruction is not a security control. Clever user input (prompt injection) can argue with your guardrails, and the model sometimes loses the argument. For real safety boundaries (blocking PII exfiltration, PII being personally identifying information like names, emails, or account numbers, enforcing access control), you need system-level controls outside the prompt: input filters, output validators, human review. That is D5 territory. D2 just needs you to know the line exists.

A natural question: does the system prompt outrank the user message?

In practice, training teaches models to treat system instructions as higher priority than user instructions. But it is a priority, not a wall. A user message that says "ignore your instructions" is the classic injection attack, and it sometimes works. So design as if system wins, but defend as if it might not: keep dangerous capabilities behind real code-level checks, not prompt text alone.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "An agent's system prompt includes per-request user IDs and timestamps at the top, above the cache breakpoint (the marked point in the prompt where caching starts). Cache hit rate is near zero." Trap: answers that add more breakpoints or raise the TTL. The credited fix: move the volatile fields below the breakpoint (or to the end), because the changing prefix is what kills the hit rate. This is the same trap as Unit 6, wearing a system-prompt costume.

What these questions really test: placement and structure. What belongs in the system prompt versus the user message. Why the static prefix matters for caching. And where prompt guardrails are insufficient: the answer is almost always "add a control outside the prompt".

Next: Unit 5, context window management: budget it like money.

How to read this diagram
  1. The green panel is what prompt rules do well: refuse disallowed requests, escalate ambiguous ones, validate output shape. Cheap steering of normal behavior.
  2. The red panel is the honest limit: prompt injection can argue with your guardrails, and the model sometimes loses the argument.
  3. Takeaway: real safety boundaries live outside the prompt, in input filters, output validators, and human review.
How to read this diagram
  1. The bigger-window trap: "give the model a bigger context window" when the real problem is history growth.
  2. The TTL trap: "raise the cache TTL" when the hit rate is near zero because the prefix changes.
  3. The co-exist trap: "add caching to fix the cost" when the cost is output tokens. Caching cannot discount output.
  4. The method: low hit rate means check prefix stability and breakpoint placement first. Cost from output tokens means cut output, not input.

Unit 5. Context window management: budget it like money

Why this unit comes next.

Unit 4 gave your application a constitution. In production, conversations grow: tool results stack up, history accumulates, and the window fills. This unit teaches you to budget the context window like money, because it is money.

On the board: your agent's conversations grow every turn. What fills the window, what breaks when it fills, and how do you keep it under control?

You will leave this unit able to budget a context window and name the techniques that keep long sessions working.

What the context window is

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. The context window is the total number of tokens the model can consider in a single request. It covers everything you send in plus everything the model can write out. Current sizes: 1M tokens for Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, and Sonnet 5. 200K for Haiku 4.5. Max output is 128K on the big three, 64K on Haiku.

For scale, 1M tokens is roughly 750,000 English words, thousands of pages. That sounds infinite until a long agentic session starts stacking tool results.

[  everything you send in  +  everything it may write out  ]  <= window size
   system, messages, tool results, retrieved docs              1M (big three)
   thinking blocks, text answers                               200K (Haiku)

where: everything you send in = system prompt, messages, tool results, retrieved docs, thinking blocks. Everything it may write out = the max output tokens you allow. Window size = 1M tokens on Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, and Sonnet 5, and 200K on Haiku 4.5.

Worked example: the budget in action.

Take Fable 5.1, window = 1,000,000 tokens. A long session has stacked 600,000 tokens of history and tool results, and max output is set to 128,000. Check: 600,000 + 128,000 = 728,000, which is ≤ 1,000,000. It fits, with 272,000 tokens of headroom.

Now the agent pulls in 400,000 tokens of retrieved docs. New input total: 1,000,000. Check: 1,000,000 + 128,000 = 1,128,000, which is > 1,000,000. It fails. Something must give: summarize the history, drop stale tool results, or lower max output. That is the budget doing its job.

How to read this diagram
  1. The blue banner is the defining inequality: everything you send in plus everything it may write out must fit the window. 1M tokens on the big three, 200K on Haiku.
  2. The three cards are the three pains in order. Cost grows quadratically with session length. The middle of long contexts gets used less reliably. The hard wall drops or fails the request.
  3. Takeaway: a window you can fill is not a window you should fill.

Why it needs managing

Rung 2: one level deeper. Three reasons, in order of pain:

  1. Cost. In a conversation, the whole history is re-sent every turn. Turn 20 of a session re-sends turns 1 through 19 as input. Long sessions get expensive fast, and the growth is quadratic in session length, not linear.
  2. Quality. Models pay less attention to the middle of very long contexts (the "lost in the middle" effect). A key fact buried at token 400,000 of 1M is less reliably used than the same fact at the start or end. A window you can fill is not a window you should fill.
  3. The hard wall. Cross the limit and the request fails or old content is silently dropped. Either way, the agent loses information it needed.

What fills the window

The official diagram below shows the mechanics: each turn's input (system, user messages) plus output (thinking, text) all become next turn's input. Add tool results (a file read can dump thousands of tokens), retrieved documents, and few-shot examples, and a coding agent can burn 100K+ tokens in a handful of turns.

Reasoning itself is one of those consumers. The official docs diagram below shows how thinking blocks (the extended reasoning from Unit 3) become part of the next turn's input:

How to read this diagram
  1. Each turn has an input block (system plus user messages, in tan) and an output block (thinking in dark gray plus the text response, in light gray).
  2. Follow the arrows right: each turn's full input and output become part of the next turn's input. The tan input block grows every turn.
  3. The dark "Thinking" boxes are the key: extended reasoning is output, and output from earlier turns becomes input you pay to re-send later.
  4. The dashed "Context window" line at the bottom with the scissors shows the hard limit (1M tokens, or 200K on Haiku). When the growing history crosses it, old content gets cut.
  5. Teaching point: heavy thinking on every turn of a long conversation compounds twice, in context usage and in cost.

How to read this diagram
  1. Start at Turn 1: a small input (user message) and a small output (text response).
  2. Follow the arrows to Turn 2: the previous turn's input and output are now inside the new input block (tan). The input grows even though the new user message is the same size.
  3. Turn 3 shows the compounding: three turns of history stacked in one input block.
  4. The dashed line at the bottom with the scissors is the window limit: everything above it fits. Below it gets cut.
  5. Teaching point: the growth is automatic and invisible to the user. Without management (summarization, truncation), every long session eventually hits the scissors.

The management toolkit

Rung 3: the full picture. Six moves, each matched to a cause:

  • Put key facts at the start or end. Because of lost-in-the-middle, the most decision-relevant content belongs at the edges of the context, not buried in the middle of a document dump.
  • Retrieve, do not stuff. Instead of pasting a whole corpus, retrieve the few relevant chunks per request. This is RAG, retrieval-augmented generation: fetching relevant documents and feeding them into the prompt. D3's territory. Smaller, more relevant context beats bigger context on both cost and accuracy.
  • Summarize old turns (compaction). Periodically replace early conversation history with a concise summary. You trade perfect recall of old turns for a much smaller window. Note the trade: summarization itself costs a full round trip, so do it strategically, not every turn.
  • Prune tool results. Cap file reads, truncate verbose outputs, keep only the relevant excerpt. Tool results are the fastest-growing context consumer in agentic systems.
  • Keep headroom for output. Budget the window as input plus the maximum output you might need. An agent that fills 950K of a 1M window with input has no room left to write a 128K answer.
  • Scenario shape: "A coding agent's sessions slow down and get pricier the longer they run. By turn 30 the agent starts forgetting early instructions." Trap: answers that switch to a bigger context model or raise output limits. The credited moves are compaction of old turns plus pruning of tool results. The problem is history growth with no bound, not the window size.
How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "A coding agent's sessions slow down and get pricier the longer they run. By turn 30 the agent starts forgetting early instructions." Trap: answers that switch to a bigger context model or raise output limits. The credited moves are compaction of old turns plus pruning of tool results. The problem is history growth with no bound, not the window size.

What these questions test: the growth mechanics (why turn 20 costs more than turn 1), the quality argument for keeping context lean, and which technique fits the scenario. Summarization fits long conversations. Retrieval fits large corpora. Pruning fits tool-heavy agents. One classic constraint: Haiku's 200K window disqualifies it for document-heavy jobs.

Next: Unit 6, prompt caching: the cheapest big lever.

How to read this diagram
  1. Each card is one move with its cause. Key facts at the edges fight lost-in-the-middle. Retrieve instead of stuffing for large corpora. Summarize for long conversations.
  2. Pruning targets tool results, the fastest-growing consumer. Headroom reserves space for the answer. Caching keeps the static prefix cheap.
  3. Takeaway: when sessions slow down and get forgetful, the credited moves are compaction plus pruning, not a bigger model.
How to read this diagram
  1. The two cards split the bill. Input tokens are everything you send in, at 2 dollars per million on Sonnet. Output tokens are everything the model writes, at 10 dollars per million.
  2. The 5x badge is the price ratio. It holds on every model: output always costs about five times input.
  3. The consequence: anything that makes the model write more costs 5x. Long answers, chain-of-thought, verbose formats.
  4. What breaks: optimizing input tokens while ignoring output. The bill lives in what the model writes.

Unit 6. Prompt caching: the cheapest big lever

Why this unit comes next.

Unit 5 showed that the same stable prefix is re-sent and re-billed on every request. That is a solvable waste. This unit introduces prompt caching: pay for the prefix once, then read it back at a tenth of the price.

On the board: your agent re-sends the same 8,000-token system prompt on every request, a million times a day. How do you stop paying full price for it?

You will leave this unit able to explain exact-prefix caching, place breakpoints correctly, and compute the savings.

What prompt caching is

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. Prompt caching lets the API reuse work it already did. When the start of your prompt (the prefix) is identical to a recent request, the model skips reprocessing it. You pay a small fraction of the normal input price for those tokens. Think of it like a print shop: the first copy pays for typesetting, reprints pay almost nothing. It is the single biggest cost lever in most production Claude systems, routinely cutting input spend by 70 to 90 percent on repeated prefixes.

request 1:  [8,000-token static prefix] + [500 fresh]  -> pays full price (the write)
request 2:  [8,000-token static prefix] + [500 fresh]  -> prefix read at ~0.1x price
request 3:  [8,000-token static prefix] + [500 fresh]  -> prefix read at ~0.1x price

Why it exists

Production prompts are mostly repetition. The system prompt, tool definitions, few-shot examples, and retrieved background stay the same across thousands of requests. Only the last user message changes. Without caching, you pay full input price to reprocess identical tokens every time. Caching turns that repetition into a discount.

How it works under the hood

Rung 2: one level deeper. Two ways to turn it on, then the five mechanics the exam tests.

  • Automatic caching: one cache_control field at the top level of the request. The system puts the breakpoint on the last cacheable block and moves it forward as the conversation grows. Best for multi-turn chats.
  • Explicit breakpoints: cache_control on individual content blocks, for fine control. Up to 4 breakpoints per request. Automatic caching consumes one of the four slots.

The mechanics that matter for the exam:

  1. Prefix order stays fixed: tools, then system, then messages. Static content belongs early. That is also where it caches best.
  2. Matching is exact-prefix. The system hashes the prompt up to your breakpoint. One changed byte anywhere before the breakpoint (a timestamp, a reordered block) means a different hash, which means a miss.
  3. Writes happen only at breakpoints. Marking a block writes exactly one cache entry for the prefix ending there. Earlier positions get no cache writes.
  4. Reads walk backward, up to 20 blocks. On a miss at your breakpoint, the system checks earlier positions for an entry a prior request wrote. It finds prior writes, not stable content: if no earlier request wrote an entry there, there is nothing to find.
  5. TTL: 5 minutes by default, refreshed free each time the entry is hit. A 1-hour TTL is available at 2x the base input price.
How to read this diagram
  1. The blue banner holds the mechanics the exam tests: prefix order stays fixed as tools, system, messages. Static content belongs early. Matching is exact-prefix.
  2. One changed byte before the breakpoint, a timestamp or a reordered block, means a miss. Automatic caching moves the breakpoint forward. Explicit breakpoints give fine control with up to four slots.
  3. Takeaway: the KV cache stores the computed attention state for the prefix, so a hit skips reprocessing those tokens.

The price table (per million tokens)

5-minute cache write = 1.25 × base input price (paid once per TTL window)
cache read = 0.025× to 0.1× base input price (paid per hit; cheaper on the bigger tiers)

Rules of thumb: a 5-minute write costs 1.25x base input, a read costs 0.1x (cheaper on Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1). Breakpoints themselves are free. You pay only for tokens the system writes and reads.

The minimum cacheable length is 512 tokens for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5. It is 1,024 for Sonnet 5, and 4,096 for Haiku 4.5. Shorter prompts silently skip caching. If both cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens are zero in the response usage, the system cached nothing.
Model Input 5-min write 1-hour write Cache read
Fable 5.1 $10 $12.50 $20 $0.25 (0.025x)
Opus 5.5 $4 $5 $8 $0.20 (0.05x)
Sonnet 5 $2 $2.50 $4 $0.20 (0.1x)
Haiku 4.5 $1 $1.25 $2 $0.10 (0.1x)

Rules of thumb: a 5-minute write costs 1.25x base input, a read costs 0.1x (cheaper on Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1). Breakpoints themselves are free. You pay only for tokens the system writes and reads.

The minimum cacheable length is 512 tokens for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5. It is 1,024 for Sonnet 5, and 4,096 for Haiku 4.5. Shorter prompts silently skip caching. If both cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens are zero in the response usage, the system cached nothing.

How to read this diagram
  1. The long blue bar is full-price input at 1.0x. The short green bar is a cache read at 0.1x: the same tokens, one tenth the price.
  2. The amber bar is a cache write at 1.25x: the one-time cost of storing the prefix for later hits.
  3. Takeaway: when most of the prompt is a cache read, the bill collapses. That is the 76 percent saving in the worked example.

Worked example: the 76% saving

A support agent: 8,000-token static system prompt, 500 fresh tokens per request, 200 output tokens, Sonnet 5. One million requests a day at high enough frequency that reads hit.

  • No cache: 8,500 input × $2/M = $0.017, plus 200 output × $10/M = $0.002. Total $0.019/request, or $19,000/day.
  • With cache: 8,000 cached × $0.20/M = $0.0016, plus 500 fresh × $2/M = $0.001, plus output $0.002. Total $0.0046/request, or $4,600/day.
  • The write cost: 8,000 × $2.50/M = $0.02 per write, once per 5 minutes (about 288 writes a day), roughly $5.76/day. Negligible at this volume.

Saving: about 76%, roughly $14,400 a day. This is why caching is the first optimization an architect reaches for, before model switching.

How to read this diagram
  1. Each row is one request's prompt, split into colored regions. Tan is a cache read (cheap). Lavender is a 1-hour cache write. Blue is a 5-minute cache write. Gray is the uncached remainder.
  2. Top row: the prefix hit at the 1h breakpoint (arrow "1h hit (A)") but missed at later ones. The system writes new entries for the changed middle sections.
  3. Middle row: no 1h hit at all ("(A is zero)"), so the system writes the whole static section fresh at 1h TTL.
  4. Bottom row: a full 5-minute hit ("5m hit (A, B, C)"), the cheapest case: almost the entire prompt served from cache.
  5. Teaching point: different sections change at different speeds, so they earn different TTLs. Match the TTL to how often the content actually changes.

The classic trap: the breakpoint on changing content

Rung 3: the full picture: the trap everyone hits. The docs call this one out explicitly because everyone hits it. Your prompt has a large static system context, then a block with a per-request timestamp and the user message. You put the breakpoint on that last block. Request 1 writes a cache entry whose hash includes the timestamp.

Request 2 has a different timestamp, so the hash differs: miss. The 20-block lookback walks backward, but no earlier request ever wrote an entry at those earlier positions, so it finds nothing. You pay for a fresh write on every request and never get a read.

The fix: put the breakpoint at the end of the static prefix, before anything that changes per request. Automatic caching hits the same trap (it targets the last cacheable block, which may be the changing one), so prefer an explicit breakpoint on the static section in that layout.

How to read this diagram
  1. Left ("miss"): the breakpoint flag sits after the timestamp block, which changes every request. The red X marks the consequence: prefix hash differs each time, so every request is a write and a miss. Coins fall away.
  2. Right ("hit"): the same blocks, but the flag sits before the timestamp. The static prefix hash is identical across requests, so request 2 onward reads from cache. That saves coins.
  3. The block order is identical in both. Only the flag position changed. Placement is the entire game.
  4. Teaching point: when a cache "does not work," check what sits before the breakpoint before touching TTLs or adding more breakpoints.
How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "An agent caches its system prompt but the hit rate is 2%. The prompt starts with tool definitions, then a 6,000-token policy document, then a per-request session ID block. One breakpoint sits after the session block." Trap: answers that increase the TTL to 1 hour or add three more breakpoints. The credited fix is one moved breakpoint. Place it after the policy document, before the session ID. The session ID poisons the prefix hash on every request.

What these questions test: caching questions are diagnosis questions: low hit rate, which fix? The credited answer is about prefix stability and breakpoint placement, not about TTL values. Two more testable numbers: the 4-breakpoint limit (a fifth explicit breakpoint, or automatic caching when four explicit ones are already set, returns a 400 error) and the minimum-length thresholds. The API never errors when caching silently does nothing. It just bills you full price. Verify with the usage fields, not with hope.

Next: Unit 7, prompt reuse: modular prompts and Skills.

Unit 7. Prompt reuse: modular prompts and Skills

Why this unit comes next.

Unit 6 made one prompt cheap to repeat. Real applications have dozens of prompts, and a mega-prompt that does everything becomes unmaintainable. This unit answers how to organize prompts like code: modular pieces and Skills.

On the board: five agents share most of their instructions, but each drifts as people copy-paste. How do you keep one source of truth without stuffing everything into every prompt?

You will leave this unit able to design modular prompt systems and explain what Skills are and when they beat a mega-prompt.

How to read this diagram
  1. Automatic: one cache_control field at the top level. The breakpoint rides the last cacheable block as chat grows. Best for multi-turn chats.
  2. Explicit: cache_control on individual content blocks. You get up to 4 breakpoints per request, and automatic consumes one slot. Best for fine control.
  3. The warning: automatic targets the last cacheable block, which may be the changing one. Prefer an explicit breakpoint at the end of the static prefix.

What modular prompts are

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. Modular prompts break instructions into small, versioned pieces composed per task: a role module, a policy module, a format module, a domain module. Instead of one 10,000-token prompt pasted everywhere, each agent assembles the modules it needs. Change the refund policy once, and every agent that includes the policy module picks it up.

BEFORE (copy-paste):            AFTER (modules):
agent1: [10K blob, drifted]     agent1: [role][policy][format]
agent2: [10K blob, drifted]     agent2: [role][policy][domain]
agent3: [10K blob, drifted]     agent3: [role][format][domain]
change policy -> edit 3 blobs   change policy -> edit [policy] once

Why modularity exists

Copy-paste prompts rot. Five copies of the same instructions become five slightly different instructions within a quarter, and nobody knows which one is canonical. Modules give you what functions gave code: one definition, many uses, independent testing. You can eval a single module (does the format module produce valid JSON?) without running the whole agent.

How to structure it

  • Stable modules up front. Role and policy modules rarely change: put them first so they form the cached static prefix (Unit 6).
  • Volatile modules last. Per-request context goes after the cache breakpoint.
  • Version like code. Modules live in source control with change review. A prompt change is a deployment: test the rendered prompt on evals before shipping.
  • Keep modules small and single-purpose. A module that tries to cover everything becomes the mega-prompt you wanted to escape.
How to read this diagram
  1. The chain runs from stable modules on the left to volatile per-request context on the right. The green line marks the cached static prefix: stable modules first.
  2. The rules below: version like code, test the rendered prompt on evals before shipping, and keep modules small and single-purpose.
  3. Takeaway: a module that tries to cover everything becomes the mega-prompt you wanted to escape.
How to read this diagram
  1. The drift: 12 agents share compliance text, copy-pasted into each prompt. Updates take weeks. Agents disagree.
  2. The fix has two moves: extract the text into versioned modules (or a Skill). Put stable content first so it forms a cacheable prefix.
  3. The traps: "one giant shared prompt" fixes drift but taxes every request. "Fine-tune a custom model" is overkill for a copy-paste problem.

What Skills are

Rung 2: one level deeper. A Skill is a packaged unit of expertise: a folder containing a SKILL.md file (name, description, instructions) plus supporting resources such as scripts, templates, and reference files. The model reads the Skill's description and loads the full Skill only when the task matches. Think of it as an on-demand expert you can install: document-processing workflows, brand voice guidelines, data-analysis runbooks.

Why Skills beat the mega-prompt

The alternative to Skills: stuffing every capability into the system prompt. There it consumes context and money on every request, whether the request needs it or not. Skills invert this: the description is tiny and always visible, while the full instructions load only when relevant. Ten Skills cost almost nothing until used. Ten mega-prompt sections cost context on every turn. Skills are also shareable and versioned: a team installs the same Skill folder and every agent gets the same expertise.

One limit to keep straight: a Skill is instructions plus resources. It does not execute code by itself. The model still does the work, optionally using tools the Skill describes. If a scenario needs a guaranteed action (not a best effort), that guarantee belongs in code outside the model, not in a Skill.

How to read this diagram
  1. Left: the Skill folder holds three things: SKILL.md (the instructions and description), scripts (executable helpers), and resources (templates, references).
  2. The arrow to the model carries the key idea: "loads on demand". The model always sees the short description. It pulls the full Skill only when the task matches.
  3. The timeline below shows the payoff: at session start the Skill costs nothing (dashed empty box). When a matching task arrives, it loads.
  4. Teaching point: Skills are how you scale expertise across agents without scaling every prompt's token cost.
A natural question: are Skills the same as tools?

No. A tool is a function the model can call (search, run code, fetch a page): it does something. A Skill packages knowledge about how to do something well: the instructions, scripts, and resources for a domain workflow. They compose: a Skill can teach the model when and how to use your tools. The exam tests this distinction by describing a scenario and asking which mechanism fits.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "A team maintains 12 agents. The team copy-pastes shared compliance instructions into each system prompt. Updates take weeks and agents disagree." Select two.

Trap: options like "consolidate into one giant shared prompt" (fixes drift but taxes every request) or "fine-tune a custom model" (overkill). The credited pair has two moves. Extract the shared instructions into versioned modules (or a Skill). Place the stable shared content at the front of each prompt so it forms a cacheable prefix.

Next: Unit 8, the selection framework: the cheapest model that passes.

Unit 8. The selection framework: the cheapest model that passes

Why this unit comes next.

Units 1 through 7 built your prompting and context toolkit. One decision ties them together: which model do you deploy? This unit gives the selection framework: the cheapest model that passes your eval.

On the board: two candidate models both look fine in a demo. How do you decide, and how do you defend the choice to a stakeholder?

You will leave this unit with a repeatable selection procedure and the cost math to justify it.

How to read this diagram
  1. A tool is a function the model can call: search, run code, fetch a page. It does something.
  2. A Skill packages knowledge: SKILL.md plus scripts plus resources. It teaches how to do something well.
  3. They compose: a Skill can teach the model when and how to use tools.
  4. What breaks: confusing the two. Match doing versus knowing when the exam asks which one fits.

What the framework is

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. A decision procedure, not a vibe. Rank the candidates by cost and speed, then walk up the ladder only when measurements (not hunches) say the cheaper tier fails. Start at Haiku, climb only on measured failure, stop the moment a tier passes. Fable sits at the bottom as the last resort, not the default.

Rung 2: the procedure, step by step.

  1. Write the bar down first. Accuracy target, latency budget, cost ceiling. Example: "at least 90% correct on our ticket labels, p95 latency under 800 ms (p95: the latency that 95% of requests beat. It measures the slow tail, not the average), under $5,000 a month."
  2. Start at the bottom. Prototype on Haiku with a good prompt (Units 3 and 4). Measure on a representative eval set (evaluation is D4's territory. Here just know you need one).
  3. Climb only on evidence. If Haiku misses the bar, try Sonnet with the same eval. Then Opus. Fable is the last resort for reasoning-heavy work.
  4. Check the other constraints. A model can pass accuracy and still fail latency (too slow for a chat UI) or context (Haiku's 200K window is too small for your 500K-token document job).
How to read this diagram
  1. Step 1: write the bar down first, accuracy target, latency budget, cost ceiling. Step 2: prototype on Haiku and measure on a representative eval set.
  2. Step 3: climb only on measured failure, Haiku to Sonnet to Opus. Fable is the last resort, never the default.
  3. Takeaway: re-run the ladder quarterly. Selection is a recurring decision, not a one-time one.

Why this order matters

Cost gaps between tiers are multiples, not percentages. And in production, volume multiplies everything. A "slightly better" model that costs 5x is a budget decision, so it needs budget-grade evidence: measured quality on your data, not a demo impression.

One more habit the exam rewards: do not pick the model once and forget it. Models get cheaper and smarter, prices move, and your traffic mix changes. Re-run the ladder quarterly: the tier that was right in January may be overkill (or underpowered) by July. Selection is a recurring decision, not a one-time one.

Worked example: the $31,500 question

Rung 2: one level deeper: the math that makes the discipline real. A support chatbot. Each turn sends about 2,000 input tokens and gets about 300 output tokens. One million turns a month. Cost per turn:
Model Input (2,000 tok) Output (300 tok) Per turn Per month (1M turns)
Haiku 4.5 2,000 × $1/M = $0.0020 300 × $5/M = $0.0015 $0.0035 $3,500
Sonnet 5 2,000 × $2/M = $0.0040 300 × $10/M = $0.0030 $0.0070 $7,000
Opus 5.5 2,000 × $4/M = $0.0080 300 × $20/M = $0.0060 $0.0140 $14,000
Fable 5.1 2,000 × $10/M = $0.0200 300 × $50/M = $0.0150 $0.0350 $35,000

If Haiku clears the quality bar, choosing Fable burns an extra $31,500 every month for nothing. This is the archetypal D2 exam trap: a scenario where the biggest model "feels safest" but a stated constraint (cost ceiling, or a modest accuracy bar already met) points to a smaller tier.

How to read this diagram
  1. Each bar is the monthly bill for one million turns: Haiku $3,500, Sonnet $7,000, Opus $14,000, Fable $35,000. Same turns, same tokens, ten times the money.
  2. The bars scale with cost, so the Fable bar dwarfs the Haiku bar. That visual gap is the discipline made visible.
  3. Takeaway: if Haiku clears the quality bar, Fable burns $31,500 extra every month for nothing. The biggest model feels safest, but the constraint points to a smaller tier.
How to read this diagram
  1. The symptom: slower and pricier by turn 30.
  2. The cause: unbounded history growth. Tool results pile up in the window.
  3. The credited moves: compaction (summarize old turns) and pruning (drop stale tool results).
  4. The traps: switching to a bigger context model (the window is not the problem) and raising output limits (that does not touch history growth).

Latency and effort, briefly

Rung 3: the full picture. Two side constraints that can disqualify a model even when it passes the quality bar.

LATENCY: Haiku fastest -> Fable slowest
  chat UI where users wait = hard constraint (can rule out the smartest model)
  overnight batch         = barely matters, cost dominates

EFFORT (thinking budget): more thinking = better reasoning + more latency + more cost
  raise effort only where evals show it moves the metric
  never pay for deep thinking on classification

Latency roughly follows the speed column: Haiku answers fastest, Fable slowest. For a chat UI where users wait, latency is a hard constraint that can rule out the smartest model. For overnight batch jobs, latency barely matters and cost dominates.

Effort levels (adaptive or extended thinking) let a model spend more compute thinking before it answers. Higher effort buys reasoning quality at the price of latency and output tokens. The architect's call: raise effort only on the tasks where evals show it moves the metric. Do not pay for deep thinking on classification.

How to read this diagram
  1. Start at the top: write the quality bar before touching any model.
  2. Follow the "no" arrows downward: each failure moves you one rung up the price ladder.
  3. Each "yes" exits right to "ship it": stop climbing the moment a tier passes. That is the whole discipline.
  4. The two side boxes (latency budget, cost ceiling) feed every decision: a model can pass evals and still fail on those boxes.
  5. Teaching point: Fable sits at the bottom as the last resort, not the default. The exam rewards restraint.
How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "An overnight batch job summarizes 50K documents. No latency requirement. Budget $2,000 a month. Sonnet prototype costs $4,800."

Trap: answers that keep Sonnet and cut corners elsewhere. The credited move: test Haiku on the summarization eval. No latency constraint forces a faster tier. The cost ceiling is the binding constraint.

The reading move: read the constraint before the options. Accuracy SLA, latency budget, cost ceiling, context size. Two or three options will be defensible in the abstract. Only one satisfies every stated constraint at the lowest cost.

Practice scenarios

Why this section comes next.

Eight units of technique. Now the exam format: scenarios that mix prompting, context, and cost decisions. Work these before the full question bank.

Two items in exam style. Each states how many to select. Answers and reasoning follow.

Scenario 1 (select one)

A medical triage assistant must classify incoming messages into five urgency levels. Requirement: at least 92% accuracy, p95 latency under 1 second, 3M requests a month, tight cost ceiling. A prototype on Sonnet 5 with zero-shot prompting hits 93.5% accuracy at 600 ms p95. What should the architect do next?

A. Ship the Sonnet prototype. It meets every stated constraint. B. Move to Opus 5.5 for a safety margin above 92%. C. Add chain-of-thought to push accuracy higher. D. Test Haiku 4.5 with few-shot examples against the 92% bar before deciding.

Reveal answer and reasoning

Answer: D. The prototype already passes, but the selection framework (Unit 8) says to check the cheaper tier before committing. Haiku at 3M requests a month could cut the bill roughly in half versus Sonnet. Few-shot examples are the right tool if zero-shot falls slightly short on format adherence. A is defensible but not optimal: it skips the cheaper-tier check the framework requires. B violates the cost ceiling for unneeded margin. C adds output-token cost and latency for no required gain.

Scenario 2 (select two)

Answers: B and C (order does not matter). Together they do the same fix. Automatic caching targets the last cacheable block, which here is the changing customer record. The prefix hash differs every request: writes every time, hits never (Unit 6 trap).

B pins the breakpoint at the end of the static prefix. C ensures the volatile content sits after it. A changes how long entries live, but the cache serves no hits. D and E do not address prefix stability at all.

A. Raise the cache TTL to 1 hour. B. Place an explicit breakpoint at the end of the static policy section. C. Move the customer record after the breakpoint. D. Increase the number of few-shot examples. E. Switch to a larger context model.
